title: The Cauchy–Crofton Constant Decays to Zero
description: Proves that the Cauchy–Crofton constant c_n = 2σ_{n-2}/((n-1)σ_{n-1}) satisfies c_n → 0 as n → ∞. The proof uses a two-step recurrence c_{n+2} = c_n · n/(n+1) derived from the sphere area recurrence, an inductive upper bound c_n ≤ 2/√(nπ) via the AM-GM inequality n(n+2) ≤ (n+1)², and the squeeze theorem. Zero sorries, zero axioms.

overview.historicalContext: The Cauchy–Crofton formula (Cauchy 1832, Crofton 1868) relates the expected number of crossings between a curve and a random hyperplane grid. In n dimensions, the crossing constant is c_n = 2σ_{n-2}/((n-1)σ_{n-1}) where σ_k is the surface area of S^k. Santaló (1976) discusses the geometry in his classical treatise on integral geometry. The fact that c_n → 0 reflects the geometric phenomenon that in high dimensions, randomly oriented hyperplanes become increasingly unlikely to intersect a fixed curve.
overview.problemStatement:
**Open Question (OQ-01 of OQ-04)**: Does the Cauchy–Crofton constant c_n → 0 as n → ∞?

**Answer**: YES — proved in this entry via the AM-GM inequality and squeeze theorem.
overview.text: A 153-line proof that the dimension-dependent crossing constant c_n decays to zero. The key insight is a two-step recurrence c_{n+2} = c_n · n/(n+1) derived from the sphere area recurrence σ_n = 2π/(n-1)·σ_{n-2}. Combined with the AM-GM estimate n(n+2) ≤ (n+1)², this gives the upper bound c_n ≤ 2/√(nπ), which tends to zero by the squeeze theorem.
overview.proofStrategy: Step 1: Derive c_{n+2} = c_n · n/(n+1) from the sphere area recurrence. Step 2: Prove 2/√(nπ) is an upper bound for c_n by induction on even and odd subsequences, using the key geometric inequality n · √((n+2)π) ≤ (n+1) · √(nπ). This reduces (by squaring) to n(n+2) ≤ (n+1)², which is AM-GM. Step 3: Apply the squeeze theorem: 0 ≤ c_n ≤ 2/√(nπ) → 0.
keyInsights: The two-step recurrence c_{n+2} = c_n · n/(n+1) follows algebraically from two applications of the sphere area recurrence σ_n = 2π/(n-1)·σ_{n-2}
The AM-GM inequality n(n+2) ≤ (n+1)² is the arithmetic heart: it bounds n/(n+1) ≤ √(n/(n+2))
The inductive bound c_n ≤ 2/√(nπ) is tight at n=2 (where c_2 = 2/π and 2/√(2π) ≈ 0.798)
The squeeze theorem requires showing 2/√(nπ) → 0, which follows from sqrt(nπ) → ∞ and inv_tendsto_atTop_zero

sections.title: Two-Step Recurrence
sections.summary: Proves c_{n+2} = c_n · n/(n+1) for n ≥ 2. Uses sphereArea_recurrence at n and n+1 to eliminate sphere area terms via field_simp and ring.
sections.mathContext: c_{n+2} = 2σ_n/((n+1)σ_{n+1}). Substituting σ_n = 2π/(n-1)·σ_{n-2} and σ_{n+1} = 2π/n·σ_{n-1}: factors cancel to give c_n · n/(n+1).

sections.title: Key Geometric Inequality
sections.summary: Proves n·√((n+2)π) ≤ (n+1)·√(nπ) by squaring: reduces to n(n+2) ≤ (n+1)² (AM-GM).
sections.mathContext: Squaring both sides: n²·(n+2)π ≤ (n+1)²·nπ, i.e., n(n+2) ≤ (n+1)². This holds since (n+1)² - n(n+2) = 1 > 0.

sections.title: Inductive Upper Bound
sections.summary: Proves c_n ≤ 2/√(nπ) for n ≥ 2 by simultaneous induction on even (2+2k) and odd (3+2k) subsequences. Base cases c_2 = 2/π and c_3 = 1/2 verified by nlinarith with sq_sqrt hints.
sections.mathContext: Inductive step: c_{n+2} = c_n·n/(n+1) ≤ (2/√(nπ))·n/(n+1) ≤ 2/√((n+2)π). The last step uses div_mul_div_comm and div_le_div_iff to reduce to the geometric inequality.

sections.title: Main Theorem via Squeeze
sections.summary: Proves Tendsto cauchyCroftonConst atTop (nhds 0) via squeeze: 0 ≤ c_n ≤ 2/√(nπ) and 2/√(nπ) → 0.
sections.mathContext: 2/√(nπ) = 2·(sqrt(nπ))⁻¹. Since nπ → ∞, sqrt(nπ) → ∞ (Real.tendsto_sqrt_atTop), hence (sqrt(nπ))⁻¹ → 0 (tendsto_inv_atTop_zero). Multiplying by 2 and applying squeeze gives the result.

conclusion.summary: The Cauchy–Crofton constant c_n → 0 as n → ∞, proved using the two-step recurrence c_{n+2} = c_n·n/(n+1), the AM-GM bound c_n ≤ 2/√(nπ), and the squeeze theorem. This resolves the sorry in the parent entry (buffons-needle-oq-01-oq-01-oq-04).
conclusion.implications: In high dimensions, random hyperplane crossings become increasingly rare for a fixed-length curve. This has implications for probabilistic geometry in high-dimensional spaces, where phenomena analogous to the curse of dimensionality appear in integral geometry.
